3	# First Principles Analysis Output Template
4	
5	> **Note:** This is the full annotated template with complete section guidance, type
6	> definitions, and prescriptions. A condensed skeleton showing just the required section
7	> names and chain format lives resident in the agent body (`SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface) for quick reference. Come here
8	> for the complete instructions when authoring or reviewing an analysis.
9	
10	## How to Use This Template
11	
12	This template is a **strict-shape document**. All six sections must be present in the fixed order below. No section may be omitted.
13	
14	If a section has no genuine content for a given analysis — because the problem is simple, the domain has no relevant dead ends, or the section truly does not apply — mark it with the honest-depth escape valve:
15	
16	> `Nothing material here — [reason explaining why this section has no content for this particular analysis and that the omission is justified, not lazy]`
17	
18	The section heading must still appear. The escape valve exists to prevent box-ticking fabrication: it is always better to write `Nothing material here — [reason]` than to fill a section with words that say nothing.
19	
20	**Section order (fixed):**
21	1. Problem Essence
22	2. Assumptions Table
23	3. Ground Truths
24	4. Derivation Chains
25	5. Abandoned Reasoning
26	6. Conclusion
27	
28	---
29	
30	## 1. Problem Essence
31	
32	State the core problem in a single sentence — not the symptoms, not the solution space, but the irreducible question the analysis must answer.
33	
34	**Core problem:** [One sentence. Strip away implementation details and surface the underlying question.]
35	
36	**Success criteria:** [Measurable, observable outcomes that would confirm the problem is solved. A skeptic must be able to verify these without asking for further clarification.]
37	
38	---
39	
40	## 2. Assumptions Table
41	
42	List every assumption — explicit and implicit — that the analysis rests on. Classify each by type and apply the prescribed treatment. An assumption omitted from this table is an assumption that will propagate unchallenged through every later step.
43	
44	| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
45	|------------|------|-----------|---------|--------------|
46	| [Assumption text] | [physical law / current constraint / convention / untested belief] | [prescribed action per type — see below] | [Accept / Challenge / Discard] — [justification/reason] | [source, or "unverified — flagged" if used in a chain per D-07] |
47	
48	### Type Definitions and Prescribed Treatments
49	
50	**physical law** — a constraint imposed by physics, mathematics, or formal logic that cannot change regardless of context or decisions made.
51	Prescribed treatment: accept as a ground-truth candidate and record it in the Ground Truths section.
52	
53	**current constraint** — a real limitation that applies now but could change (budget, team size, regulatory environment, technology availability).
54	Prescribed treatment: record the expiry conditions — what would have to change for this constraint to no longer hold. Do not treat it as permanent.
55	
56	**convention** — a practice or standard that exists because it has been adopted, not because it is physically or logically required.
57	Prescribed treatment: explicitly challenge the convention before accepting it. "We do it this way" is not a justification.
58	
59	**untested belief** — a claim held as true that has not been empirically verified in the context of this analysis.
60	Prescribed treatment: verify it, or flag it unverified. An untested belief used in a derivation chain must be marked with the `GT-N?` notation (see Ground Truths) and any conclusion depending on it inherits a confidence caveat.
61	
62	### Stakes-Escalation Rule
63	
64	The higher the stakes of the conclusion resting on an assumption, the more that assumption must be pushed toward physical law or verified ground truth status. Classification drives the method — it does not merely label.
65	
66	### Verdict Vocabulary
67	
68	The Verdict cell is a token prefix followed by an em-dash and the justification — the bare
69	token leads so it stays matchable, and the em-dash prose carries the reasoning:
70	
71	- **Accept** — the assumption survives challenge and may be used in the analysis (e.g., "Accept — survives P2 challenge; physical-law backed by GT-1")
72	- **Challenge** — the assumption is questionable; probe further before use (e.g., "Challenge — vendor benchmark unverified, flagged GT-5?")
73	- **Discard** — the assumption is false or irrelevant; remove from the reasoning chain (e.g., "Discard — contradicted by GT-2, no longer load-bearing")
74	
75	**A current-constraint verdict records its expiry at the point of use.** An assumption classified `current constraint` is accepted only until that constraint lapses; the verdict cell says when. The expiry belongs in the em-dash justification and never in the token slot — the token slot carries one of the three tokens above and nothing else.
76	
77	**Conforming — a current constraint recording its expiry:**
78	
79	```text
80	Accept — expires at term end (1 or 3 years); until then the constraint is contractual, not physical
81	```
82	
83	**Non-conforming — the expiry hoisted into the token slot:**
84	
85	```text
86	Current constraint (expires at term end) — contractual, not physical
87	```
88	
89	The vocabulary above is unchanged because run 3 rendered four current-constraint rows conformingly on the identical prompt by putting the expiry in the justification — this is a worked example, not a schema change.
90	
91	---
92	
93	## 3. Ground Truths
94	
95	List the irreducible, verified facts the analysis builds on. Each ground truth carries a stable identifier used by the Derivation Chains section. Once assigned, an ID does not change.
96	
97	A ground truth must pass this test: it is a fact that is true regardless of what solution is chosen, verifiable independently of the analysis, and not derived from another item on this list.
98	
99	Every ground truth carries a **provenance label** answering one question: *did this analysis read the asserted figure or wording in the cited source?* The answer decides the suffix. A citation being present is not verification — a citation can name a real document and be wrong about what is in it.
100	
101	**Verified ground truth form** (provenance `read-at-source` — no suffix):
102	
103	- **GT-1** [fact text] — source: [verification source — data, measurement, published spec, direct observation]; read-at-source: [page, table, section, or quoted passage where the figure was read]
104	- **GT-2** [fact text] — source: [verification source]; read-at-source: [where read]
105	
106	**Delegate-reported ground truth form** (provenance `reported-by-delegate` — `?` required):
107	
108	- **GT-3?** [fact text] — cited to: [source the delegate named]; reported-by-delegate: [which sub-agent, search, or summary supplied it] — cited source not opened by this analysis
109	
110	**Unverified ground truth form (D-07)** (provenance `unverified` — `?` required):
111	
112	- **GT-4?** [fact text] — unverified: [specific reason the fact could not be verified in this analysis]
113	
114	The `?` suffix signals that this ground truth has not been read at its source — whether because it is an untested belief or because a delegate reported it and nobody opened the citation. Any conclusion depending on a `GT-N?` input inherits a confidence caveat in the Derivation Chains section. The analysis may proceed with such inputs — but the uncertainty must be visible.
115	
116	**The `?` is the default.** Drop it only when the read-at-source location can be named. A delegate report counts as read-at-source only when it quotes the source's own wording and that quote was checked — not when it merely supplies a well-formed citation.
117	
118	**Provenance summary (required):** enumerate the `?`-marked ground truths **by ID**, and for every unsuffixed ground truth feeding a HIGH-confidence chain, name its read-at-source location. Write the list, not a number:
119	
120	```text
121	?-marked: GT-2, GT-5, GT-9, GT-14 (4 of 22)
122	Read-at-source: GT-3 — 45 CFR 164.514(b)(2)(i), subsections (A)/(B)/(R) quoted verbatim
123	```
124	
125	A stated integer does not satisfy this — an integer cannot be checked against the list it summarizes, and an enumeration can. Where a count and its enumeration disagree, **the enumeration governs.** Neither an empty enumeration nor a count of zero satisfies this on its own; the named locations are the auditable part.
126	
127	IDs are stable once assigned. GT-3 remains GT-3 throughout the document even if GT-3 is later verified or discarded.
128	
129	---
130	
131	## 4. Derivation Chains
132	
133	Show how the ground truths combine into conclusions. Every conclusion offered in this analysis must have exactly one chain here — no more (no redundant restatement), no fewer (no orphaned conclusions).
134	
135	**Chain numbering convention.** Number each `### Conclusion:` block in this section `C1`,
136	`C2`, ... in document order (e.g., `### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]`). The §6→§4
137	closure ledger (the agent body — `SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface — "Before presenting conclusions") cites these IDs when mapping a
138	Conclusion-section (section 6) claim back to the chain in this section that established it.
139	
140	**Chain format:**
141	
142	```text
143	GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]
144	```
145	
146	The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
147	
148	Each chain must contain at least one intermediate step. A chain that goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion is incomplete — the intermediate is where the reasoning happens. The intermediate must be a new claim that could not be stated from any single head input alone. If no intermediate can be stated, the conclusion is either a restatement of a head input (trivial) or a reasoning step is missing.
149	
150	**No-wrap rule.** A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. A chain needing more hops continues on further arrow-led lines. A hop too long for comfort is SPLIT, not wrapped — the analysis renders as Markdown, so a long hop soft-wraps for the reader without breaking the form.
151	
152	```text
153	GT-1 ([brief fact label]) + GT-6 ([brief fact label])
154	→ [intermediate claim]
155	→ [further intermediate]
156	→ [conclusion]
157	```
158	
159	**Head-input rule.** The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
160	
161	```text
162	GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])
163	→ [intermediate claim]
164	→ [conclusion]
165	```
166	
167	The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
168	
169	The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples.
170	
171	**Conforming — head, then one hop per line:**
172	
173	```text
174	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
175	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
176	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
177	```
178	
179	**Non-conforming — a hop broken across physical lines:**
180	
181	```text
182	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
183	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
184	  once idle-time billing is included
185	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
186	```
187	
188	The continuation line does not begin with `→`, so the chain terminates at the head's first hop and what remains reads as an incomplete chain.
189	
190	**Non-conforming — the same hops rendered as a numbered list:**
191	
192	```text
193	1. GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
194	2. Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
195	3. sustained workloads belong on Fargate
196	```
197	
198	A numbered list restates each hop as its own GT-headed one-hop chain, which reads as several incomplete chains rather than one complete one — the intermediate steps stop being connected to the conclusion they build toward.
199	
200	**Non-conforming — an input carrying unparenthesized prose:**
201	
202	```text
203	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2's threshold
204	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
205	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
206	```
207	
208	`C2's threshold` is not an identifier — it is a possessive prose phrase — so the head does not parse; the third input must be written `C2 (threshold)`.
209	
210	**Conforming — the same head with the upstream chain as an input:**
211	
212	```text
213	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2 (threshold)
214	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
215	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
216	```
217	
218	Exactly one token differs from the block above: a `Cn` identifier with a parenthesized gloss is an admissible head input, on equal footing with a `GT-N` identifier.
219	
220	**Conforming — a chain consuming only upstream conclusions:**
221	
222	```text
223	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold) + C4 (unconditional, zero code change) + C5 (~73% ceiling, no execution-model change)
224	→ C4 and C5 deliver verified savings that do not depend on any property of your workload
225	→ C2's saving depends entirely on a duty-cycle figure nobody has measured
226	```
227	
228	A head may consist entirely of `Cn` inputs with no `GT-N` term. The second hop's `C2's saving` is prose, not a head input — the head-only scope note is what permits it here.
229	
230	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the same prose input in a non-final position:**
231	
232	```text
233	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + C2's threshold + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown)
234	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
235	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
236	```
237	
238	This head breaks the same rule as the non-conforming block above and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — with a well-formed input still to its right the check matches from `GT-12?` onward and never reaches `C2's threshold`. Write `C2 (threshold)` wherever the input sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
239	
240	**Non-conforming — a hop beginning with a GT-N identifier:**
241	
242	```text
243	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
244	→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term in both estimates
245	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
246	```
247	
248	The second line reads as the head of a new chain because it begins with a `GT-N` identifier, so this chain ends after its head and what remains is an incomplete chain — the possessive is not the problem, the leading identifier is.
249	
250	**Conforming — the same hop with the identifier moved off the front:**
251	
252	```text
253	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
254	→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term in both estimates
255	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
256	```
257	
258	Exactly one clause is reordered and the chain is whole again; naming a ground truth inside a hop is fine, leading with its identifier is not.
259	
260	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the GT-led hop in a later position:**
261	
262	```text
263	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
264	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
265	→ the second reading is the binding one
266	→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term in both estimates
267	```
268	
269	This hop breaks the same rule as the non-conforming block above and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — the check has already satisfied its two-arrow requirement on the hops that precede it, so the leading identifier ends the chain there without changing the verdict. Write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term in both estimates` wherever the hop sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
270	
271	**Non-conforming — the first hop closing its own sentence:**
272	
273	```text
274	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
275	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape.
276	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes
277	```
278	
279	This chain violates none of R1-R9 — every input parses, every hop states one inference, no hop leads with a `GT-N` identifier — and is scored malformed anyway, because the mechanical form check ends the chain the moment the first hop closes its own sentence, before its two-arrow requirement is satisfied, and never reaches the well-formed hop that follows.
280	
281	**Conforming — the same chain with the first hop's terminal period removed:**
282	
283	```text
284	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
285	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape
286	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes
287	```
288	
289	Exactly one character differs from the block above: the terminal period. Removing it, and nothing else, restores the two-arrow match the check requires.
290	
291	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the same period moved to a later hop:**
292	
293	```text
294	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
295	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape
296	→ the migration case does not rest on C1 alone
297	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes.
298	```
299	
300	This block breaks the identical rule one hop later and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — with two hops already matched before the closing sentence is reached, the check has satisfied its two-arrow requirement and the sentence-closing period on the third hop has no following line left to block. Write the closing hop with no terminal punctuation wherever it sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
301	
302	**One-inference rule.** A hop states exactly ONE inference. If a hop joins two claims with "and", or carries a parenthetical that could stand as its own claim, it is two hops — split it.
303	
304	TELL (not the rule): a hop past ~200 characters is almost always two hops. Measure the hop, then split — do not wrap it, and do not trim words to hit a number.
305	
306	Inline annotations (`*[Assumes: A14 — …]*`) attach to the end of the hop line they qualify and do not start a new hop.
307	
308	### Converting structured-technique outputs into chains
309	
310	Structured-technique outputs (trade-off matrices, second-order effect lists) do not appear in this section as-is — each converts into the chain format above using the rule for its technique below. This subsection is the single source of truth for the conversion; the per-technique Handoff sections point back here rather than restating it, so future structured techniques extend this one place.
311	
312	**Trade-off matrix → one chain.** A trade-off matrix collapses into ONE chain whose intermediate cites the winning weighted total and whose endpoint names a single recommended option:
313	
314	```text
315	GT-refs (criteria's factual basis) → weighted totals (the winning total vs. the runner-up, naming the high-weight criteria that drive it) → recommended option
316	```
317	
318	Example: `GT-2 + GT-5 (criteria facts) → weighted totals: B=82 > A=64, driven by reliability×warranty → recommend B`. The full matrix stays in the technique's own output — this subsection carries only the single collapsed chain, never the matrix re-expressed row-by-row (that would violate the one-chain-per-conclusion rule above). An exact tie between weighted totals still resolves to a single named recommended option; a tie must not produce a multi-option chain endpoint. **Exact-tie tiebreak (deterministic):** on an exact tie, prefer the option with fewer `GT-N?` (unverified) inputs among its winning criteria; if still tied, name both totals in the chain intermediate but select the first-listed option as the chain endpoint, and flag the tie explicitly in the Conclusion section's confidence line.
319	
320	**Second-order effect list → order-marked extension.** A second-order effect list extends the parent chain IN PLACE as additional order-marked steps, each carrying the same evidentiary discipline as the first-order steps that produced the conclusion:
321	
322	```text
323	GT-N → first-order conclusion →[2nd] [2nd-order effect] →[3rd] [3rd-order effect] (contradicts GT-M → back to Phase 2)
324	```
325	
326	Example: `GT-1 → first-order conclusion →[2nd] flag-config surface grows →[3rd] flag debt accumulates (contradicts GT-4 → back to P2)`. The order marks (`[2nd]`, `[3rd]`) make the extension's sequence legible. A contradicting effect routes the conclusion back to Phase 2 — never directly to Phase 3 or past Phase 2. A pass that surfaces no non-contradicting downstream effect leaves the parent chain unextended — a clean no-op, not an error.
327	
328	### Confidence levels, defined
329	
330	`HIGH`, `MEDIUM` and `LOW` name how much of a chain is **outstanding** — not how strongly the analysis believes its conclusion. Three axes decide the band, each answerable by inspecting what the chain already carries on the page:
331	
332	- **Inputs** — the provenance of every identifier on the head line: an unsuffixed `GT-N` with a named read-at-source location, a `?`-marked ground truth, or a `Cn` carrying its own band.
333	- **Inference** — whether each hop the chain's endpoint depends on follows from the line above it, or needs a premise supplied by an `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation.
334	- **Rivals** — whether a competing conclusion from the same ground truths survives, and what rules it out. Section 5 is where the ruling-out is written down, so a chain answers this axis by pointing at its own Abandoned Reasoning entry as readily as by carrying the rival on its confidence line.
335	
336	**The band is the lowest the three axes license.** A chain is not HIGH because two of them are clean.
337	
338	**HIGH — nothing on this chain is outstanding.** Every identifier on the head line is an unsuffixed `GT-N` whose read-at-source location is named, or a `Cn` itself rated HIGH; every hop the endpoint depends on follows from the line above it by deduction, by arithmetic that recomputes when redone independently of the chain text, or by a regularity cited to an unsuffixed ground truth; and the strongest rival conclusion the analysis considered is named — on this confidence line or in a section 5 entry this chain points to — together with the ground truth or chain that rules it out, that ruling-out input itself unsuffixed. A chain whose endpoint a live alternative still contests is unexamined, not certain: it is MEDIUM at best.
339	
340	An `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation on a hop shorts the Inference axis **unless** the confidence line says what becomes of the endpoint when that assumption fails and the endpoint still stands — *"A2 is that the CDN'd assets are versioned; if they were not, the CDN result would be weaker evidence still, so the conclusion is unaffected"*. An annotation on a hop that only qualifies a second-order extension, and not the endpoint, is outside this axis and the chain says which case it is. Stating the sensitivity is the work; an unexamined assumption is not the same thing as one whose falsity has been priced.
341	
342	The Rivals axis is answered when a section 5 entry names a competing conclusion to this chain's endpoint and the chain or ground truth that ruled it out, or when the endpoint is itself a ruling-out — a chain establishing that some option does not work has already done the rival's work and does not need a rival of its own. It is short when a competing conclusion has been raised anywhere in the analysis and nothing settles it, and when the analysis reaches a positive recommendation with no section 5 content bearing on it at all.
343	
344	**MEDIUM — exactly one axis is short, and the shortfall is named and bounded.** One of: an identifier on the head line is `?`-marked or is a `Cn` rated MEDIUM; or at most one hop the endpoint depends on rests on a stated `[Assumes: A-N]` premise whose failure the chain has not priced; or a rival to the endpoint is live and nothing in the analysis settles it. The confidence line names which axis is short, names the specific input, hop or rival, and states what would close it — the verification that would remove an input as a cause of the downgrade, the evidence that would establish an assumed premise, or the observation that would settle between this conclusion and its rival. A MEDIUM chain is one whose weakness a reader can point at.
345

3	# Trade-Off Analysis
4	
5	> Structures a choice between two or more genuinely viable options by weighting
6	> criteria before scoring — preventing the reverse-engineering of weights to
7	> justify a decision already made intuitively.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## When to reach for this
12	
13	Use this tool when two or more options are viable (none obviously dominant), the
14	choice spans multiple criteria that pull in different directions, and an
15	intuitive pick would be hard to justify to others.
16	
17	Do not use it when one option dominates on every relevant criterion — that is a
18	direct decision, not a trade-off.
19	
20	---
21	
22	## Procedure
23	
24	1. **Name the options.** List each option being compared.
25	
26	2. **List criteria.** Identify 5–8 criteria that matter to this decision. Lock
27	   this list — add no new criteria after this step. If a criterion matters, it
28	   must appear now.
29	
30	3. **Assign weights. Lock them now.** Give each criterion a relative weight
31	   (1–5) before scoring any option. If you cannot assign weights without first
32	   seeing how options score, stop — locking weights before scoring is the core
33	   discipline that prevents reverse-engineering them to favor an intuitive pick.
34	
35	4. **Score each option** on each criterion independently (1–5). Phrase every
36	   criterion so higher is always better (e.g., "Reliability" not "Reliability
37	   risk") — a mixed scale silently inverts the result.
38	
39	5. **Compute:** multiply weight × score per criterion; sum per option.
40	
41	6. **Read the result.** The highest weighted total is the recommendation. If
42	   it surprises you, only re-examine a weight when you can state why it was
43	   wrong *before* seeing the result — adjusting weights afterward is the
44	   failure mode this procedure prevents.
45	
46	**Sensitivity check:** If two options score within roughly 10% of each other,
47	do not refine scores. Identify the criterion whose weight, if changed, would
48	flip the result, and ask whether that weight is genuinely wrong — if not, the
49	near-tie is a real finding and either option is defensible.
50	
51	---
52	
53	## Example
54	
55	**Decision:** Laptop for a parent who browses, video-calls, and writes
56	documents — refurbished mid-range (A) vs. new entry-level (B).
57	
58	**Step 2 — criteria locked:**
59	
60	| Criterion                       | Weight |
61	|----------------------------------|--------|
62	| Performance                      | 4      |
63	| Reliability                      | 5      |
64	| Cost                             | 3      |
65	| Warranty / support               | 4      |
66	| Portability                      | 2      |
67	| Ease of setup (non-technical)    | 3      |
68	
69	**Steps 3 → 4 — weights locked, then scored independently:**
70	
71	| Option     | Performance (×4) | Reliability (×5) | Cost (×3)  | Warranty (×4) | Portability (×2) | Ease of setup (×3) | Total  |
72	|------------|------------------|------------------|------------|---------------|------------------|--------------------|--------|
73	| A (refurb) | 4 × 4 = 16       | 2 × 5 = 10       | 5 × 3 = 15 | 2 × 4 = 8     | 3 × 2 = 6        | 3 × 3 = 9          | **64** |
74	| B (new)    | 2 × 4 = 8        | 5 × 5 = 25       | 3 × 3 = 9  | 5 × 4 = 20    | 4 × 2 = 8        | 4 × 3 = 12         | **82** |
75	
76	**Result:** B (new entry-level) scores 82 vs. 64 — driven by reliability and
77	warranty, weighted high because device failure would leave the parent without
78	support. Recommendation: buy new.
79	
80	---
81	
82	## Failure modes
83	
84	- **Weights set after scoring.** If you scored options before assigning
85	  weights, the weights will unconsciously reflect the scores — discard and
86	  restart from step 3.
87	
88	- **Too many criteria.** More than 8 criteria dilute the signal toward noise —
89	  prune to those that genuinely differentiate the options.
90	
91	- **Criteria added mid-analysis.** Adding a criterion after seeing partial
92	  scores is almost always rationalizing — lock the list at step 2 and restart.
93	
94	- **Treating a near-tie as a precision problem.** Refining scores to break a
95	  near-tie manufactures false precision; run the sensitivity check instead.
96	
97	- **Criteria that are not independent.** Two criteria measuring the same factor
98	  (e.g., "cost" and "budget impact") double-count it — merge or drop one.
99	
100	---
101	
102	## Output contract
103	
104	The focused trade-off output MUST include these four level-2 section headers, verbatim,
105	as real `##` headings in the response. Strict on the header strings; soft on content.
106	This structure enables reliable downstream detection.
107	
108	Required headers:
109	
110	- `## Options`
111	- `## Criteria & Weights`
112	- `## Scoring`
113	- `## Recommendation`
114	
115	---
116	
117	## Handoff
118	
119	The output is the recommended option with its weighted justification and the
120	reasoning behind the weights. Return to Phase 4 (Reason Upward) and convert it
121	into the Derivation Chain using the trade-off collapse form defined in
122	output-template.md §4 ("Converting structured-technique outputs into chains") —
123	citing the weighted scores as the step between ground truths and conclusion.

3	# Pre-Mortem
4	
5	> A prospective-hindsight failure analysis tool. Reach for this when a proposed
6	> plan needs stress-testing before commitment — the goal is to surface probable
7	> failure causes before they materialise.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## When to reach for this
12	
13	Use a pre-mortem once a plan has enough specificity to reason about particular
14	failure modes, but before it is finalised and carries organizational momentum.
15	Not the right tool for evaluating options (use trade-off analysis) or for tracing
16	something that already went wrong (use 5-Whys).
17	
18	---
19	
20	## Framing
21	
22	Before any other step, adopt this premise explicitly:
23	
24	> It is approximately six months from now. This plan has failed — not merely
25	> underperformed, but failed badly. That outcome is a fact.
26	> Working backward: what caused it?
27	
28	This past-tense framing is not rhetorical. It bypasses the optimism bias that
29	makes forward-looking risk lists generic. Do not skip it or soften it to
30	"might fail" — the grammatical shift from possibility to accomplished fact is
31	the mechanism.
32	
33	---
34	
35	## Procedure
36	
37	1. **Restate the premise.** Before writing anything, say or write: "The plan has
38	   already failed. What caused it?" This re-anchors the prospective-hindsight
39	   frame before analysis begins.
40	
41	2. **Write independently.** List every cause of the failure without filtering —
42	   write the full list before reviewing it. Do not discard causes that seem
43	   unlikely; the list is raw material, not a verdict. Generate from at least
44	   three named viewpoints — for example the implementer, the person who has to
45	   live with the result, whoever pays for it, and a competitor who benefits
46	   from the failure. One generator asked once returns one perspective's
47	   failures, and the causes it misses are systematically the ones outside the
48	   frame it was asked in.
49	
50	3. **Interrogate the list adversarially.** Re-read each item and ask which ones
51	   contradict the plan's own stated premise, or the recommendation the analysis
52	   is about to make. A cause that would embarrass the conclusion is higher
53	   signal than one that merely adds risk to it. In a facilitated session these
54	   are the items a junior participant suppresses; written by a single analyst
55	   they are the items that get hedged into vagueness rather than dropped, so
56	   look for the softened ones, not the missing ones.
57	
58	4. **Identify recurring patterns.** Look for failure causes that cluster — the
59	   same root (over-optimistic timeline, single point of dependency, assumption
60	   never validated). A cluster is a structural weakness in the plan, not an
61	   isolated risk.
62	
63	5. **Act on findings.** Modify the plan to address the structural weaknesses, or
64	   explicitly accept the risk with a named mitigation. A pre-mortem with no
65	   downstream plan change was box-ticking.
66	
67	**Exit criterion:** The failure has been stated as having already happened, causes
68	are written from that stance, causes are clustered into structural weaknesses, and
69	every cluster has either a named plan change or an explicitly accepted risk with a
70	named mitigation. A pre-mortem that ends without one of those two outcomes per
71	cluster is box-ticking, not a finding.
72	
73	---
74	
75	## Output contract
76	
77	The exit criterion above names four things the pre-mortem must produce. This is
78	what they look like on the page, in this order:
79	
80	**Premise** — one line, past tense, stating the failure as accomplished fact.
81	Not "the plan might fail"; the grammatical shift is the mechanism, and a premise
82	written in the conditional has already lost it.
83	
84	**Causes** — the unfiltered list, one per line, written before any grouping
85	appears. The viewpoints from step 2 are visible in it: if every cause is a
86	technical one, step 2 was run once rather than three times. Writing the clusters
87	first and back-filling causes into them inverts the procedure and produces the
88	generic risk list the whole framing exists to avoid.
89	
90	**Clusters** — the structural weaknesses the causes fall into, each named, and
91	each naming the causes it absorbs. A cluster is a claim that several causes share
92	one root; a heading with one cause under it is a cause, not a cluster. When the
93	pre-mortem runs inside a first-principles analysis, each cluster also cites the
94	chain ids (`Cn`) or ground-truth ids (`GT-N`) it bears on, so the finding lands
95	somewhere a reader can check it against.
96	
97	**Disposition** — per cluster, one of exactly two things: a named plan change, or
98	an explicitly accepted risk with a named mitigation. "Worth watching", "we should
99	keep this in mind" and "a risk we accept" with nothing named after it are none of
100	the above. A cluster whose disposition is an accepted risk still names what makes
101	the risk survivable; that is what distinguishes accepting a risk from noticing one.
102	
103	A pre-mortem missing any of the four has not run. A pre-mortem whose causes list
104	is shorter than its cluster list ran backwards.
105	
106	---
107	
108	## Example
109	
110	**Plan:** Host a dinner party for twelve people in two weeks, cooking a full
111	three-course meal from scratch for the first time at this scale.
112	
113	**Framing applied:** It is two weeks from now. The dinner party has failed badly.
114	What caused it?
115	
116	**Backward-derived failure causes:**
117	- Underestimated preparation time; last two courses were served an hour late
118	- A key ingredient unavailable the day before; no substitution plan
119	- One course required equipment not owned and not sourced in advance
120	- Two guests had dietary restrictions not asked about until the day of
121	- Energy depleted by the time guests arrived; host unable to enjoy the evening
122	
123	**Pattern identified:** Every cause traces back to a single structural weakness —
124	no dry run at smaller scale and no contingency check before commitment. The plan
125	assumed novelty would resolve itself on the day.
126	
127	---
128	
129	## Failure modes
130	
131	**Forward-looking framing.** "What could go wrong?" produces a generic risk list.
132	If causes feel speculative and mild, the past-tense premise was not adopted.
133	
134	**Running it too early.** A pre-mortem on a plan with insufficient specificity
135	yields generic concerns. The plan must have enough detail to reason about
136	particular failure modes — vague plans produce vague analyses.
137	
138	**Anchoring (in group settings).** When facilitated, the most senior voice in the
139	room shapes the list. Run independent writing before any sharing — each
140	participant writes silently before the group compares lists.
141	
142	**First-speaker anchoring.** The first cause named draws subsequent thinking
143	toward it. Write exhaustively before ranking or grouping.
144	
145	**No follow-through.** A pre-mortem with no downstream plan change was
146	box-ticking. Findings must modify the plan or be explicitly accepted with
147	named mitigations.
148	
149	---
150	
151	## Handoff
152	
153	The probable failure causes identified here feed Phase 5 (Validate). Add the
154	highest-signal structural weaknesses to the adversarial validation pass — each
155	one is a weak-link candidate for the signed-off analysis to address or explicitly
156	accept.

120	## Scoring Model
121	
122	Score each of the 6 criteria using this shared 4-level scale, applied uniformly across all criteria
123	(highest to lowest):
124	
125	- **Rigorous** — the criterion's named artifact is present, structurally complete, and every
126	  entry meets the observable descriptor for this level: all required fields are populated with
127	  non-generic content, all required relationships are explicit,
128	  and every observable structural test in this criterion's Rigorous descriptor returns pass.
129	
130	- **Sound** — the criterion's named artifact is present and mostly meets the Rigorous descriptor,
131	  but one or more entries fall short in a specific, identifiable way: a field is generic or vague
132	  rather than empty, a relationship is implicit rather than absent, or one entry departs from the
133	  prescribed form without invalidating the rest.
134	
135	- **Hand-wavy** — the criterion's named artifact is present but fails the Rigorous descriptor in
136	  a pattern rather than an isolated entry: multiple fields are generic or empty, the artifact's
137	  prescribed structure is not followed, or the section uses the honest-depth escape valve with a
138	  reason that could be copy-pasted to any analysis without modification.
139	
140	- **Absent** — the criterion's named artifact is missing entirely, or the section exists but
141	  contains no content that could be scored against the artifact's descriptor (the section heading
142	  appears with nothing substantive below it).
143	
144	**Rank order (explicit):** Rigorous > Sound > Hand-wavy > Absent.
145	
146	**Gate:** Any criterion scored **Absent** fails the entire analysis — it must be revised before
147	conclusions are presented, regardless of how all other criteria score.
148	
149	**Hand-wavy cap:** Two or more criteria scored **Hand-wavy** also fails the entire analysis —
150	it must be revised before conclusions are presented. One criterion at Hand-wavy is tolerated
151	(one isolated weaker section does not indicate a systemic quality problem); two or more at
152	Hand-wavy indicates a pattern of shallow reasoning that the gate alone cannot catch, because
153	no single criterion has reached the gate-fail level.
154	
155	**Pass:** No criterion scores Absent, and at most one criterion scores Hand-wavy.
156	(Equivalently: every criterion is Sound or above, except at most one may be Hand-wavy.)
157	
158	**Escape-valve scoring (global rule, applies to every criterion):** Any section that
159	legitimately uses the honest-depth escape valve (`Nothing material here — [reason]`) is
160	scored **Rigorous** if the stated reason is specific to this analysis — it names a property
161	of this problem that makes the section's content unnecessary — and **Hand-wavy** if the
162	reason is generic or copy-pasteable to any analysis. A properly-used escape valve is
163	**never** scored Absent solely for using the escape valve: the per-criterion Absent
164	descriptors below apply to a section that is missing, empty, or filled with non-scoreable
165	content, not to a section that is honestly and specifically marked as having no material
166	content.
167	
168	**Load-bearing chain (definition):** A derivation chain is *load-bearing* if a claim in
169	the Conclusion section (output section 6) depends on it — i.e., the chain produces, or is
170	cited as support for, a conclusion the analysis actually presents. A chain that reaches
171	only an intermediate result no conclusion rests on is not load-bearing. (This is the
172	narrower scoring sense of the phrase `SKILL.md` uses informally as "load-bearing for a
173	high-stakes conclusion.")
